implementation_notes: JavaScript's event loop makes ordinary application code single-threaded, so most of what lock-freedom is for does not apply. Where it does apply - worker_threads sharing a SharedArrayBuffer - the platform provides Atomics, whose operations are sequentially consistent, and the Web Locks API, which is a blocking mutex and the more useful primitive. There is no memory-reclamation problem, because the GC handles it (with the caveat that a node still referenced by a stalled worker can be reused, so the ABA question is real but managed). Do not hand-roll lock-free structures in JavaScript: Atomics.wait is forbidden on the main thread, so the main-thread half of any such algorithm cannot exist.
idiom_name: Web Locks API for blocking exclusion; Atomics on SharedArrayBuffer across workers; never hand-rolled
pitfalls: Atomics.wait throws on the browser main thread, so a spin-wait algorithm cannot be written for the main thread at all.
SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation; without it there is no shared-memory primitive and the whole approach is unavailable.
Every Atomics operation is sequentially consistent with no ordering parameter, so a hand-written algorithm cannot be tuned and pays a full fence per operation.
A busy-wait on the main thread freezes the tab, which is a user-visible failure rather than a performance one.
alternative: navigator.locks.request for exclusion, a MessagePort for coordination between workers, and structured concurrency via promises
